Testing shallower trees (depth 3) with higher min_child_weight (8) and stronger regularization to see if restricting tree complexity reduces overfitting on rare positive overtake events compared to trial 1.
Following the improvement from depth 4 to 3 in trial 2, testing depth 2 with similar regularization to determine if even simpler decision stumps capture the key overtake signals without overfitting.
Trial 3 showed depth 2 underfits, so checking depth 5 with conservative learning rate and strong L2/L1 regularization to see if higher order feature interactions can outperform depth 3.
Since trial 4 with depth 5 achieved 0.5658, testing depth 6 with slightly increased regularization and min_child_weight to see if deeper interactions improve performance further.
Building on best trial 4 (depth 5, PR-AUC 0.5658), testing higher min_child_weight=9 to see if requiring more samples per leaf further stabilizes splits on the rare positive class.

Comparing min_child_weight=7 (trial 4, 0.5658) and min_child_weight=9 (trial 6, 0.5654), testing min_child_weight=5 to evaluate if slightly looser leaf constraints improve recall on rare positive cases.
Testing lower learning rate (0.025) and more trees (280) around trial 4's best architecture to see if a smoother gradient descent path improves generalization.
Following trial 8's best score of 0.5677, testing lower feature subsampling (0.6) to decorrelate individual trees on overtake features.
Since colsample_bytree=0.6 degraded performance in trial 9, testing 0.75 against the previous best 0.70 from trial 8.
Moving higher in colsample_bytree from 0.70 (0.5677) and 0.75 (0.5694) to 0.85 to determine if retaining more features per tree continues to boost PR-AUC.
Interpolating between 0.75 (0.5694) and 0.85 (0.5668) with colsample_bytree=0.80 to pinpoint the optimal feature subsampling fraction.
Testing row subsample=0.7 against the current best 0.8 from trial 10 to check whether added bagging noise improves PR-AUC.
Since subsample 0.7 degraded performance in trial 13, testing subsample 0.9 to evaluate if larger training subsets per tree provide better gradient estimates for minority class overtakes.
Checking fine-grained subsample=0.85 between 0.80 (0.5694) and 0.90 (0.5602) to verify if 0.80 is a sharp peak.
With subsample=0.8 and colsample=0.75 established as optimal, testing stronger L2 regularization (reg_lambda=6.0 vs 4.0) to see if further penalizing extreme leaf weights improves PR-AUC.
Following the jump from 0.5694 to 0.5721 with reg_lambda=6.0, testing reg_lambda=8.0 to see if even higher L2 regularization continues the trend.
Testing reg_lambda=5.0 between 4.0 (0.5694) and 6.0 (0.5721) to check if the optimum lies in this narrower interval.
Testing reg_lambda=7.0 to explore the upper side of the peak at 6.0 (0.5721) before it dropped at 8.0 (0.5686).
With reg_lambda=6.0 identified as optimal, testing higher L1 regularization (reg_alpha=0.4 vs 0.2) to induce sparser tree weights and reduce noise from uninformative features.
Testing lower L1 regularization (reg_alpha=0.1 vs 0.2 and 0.4) to determine if lighter sparsity penalty retains subtle overtake interaction signals.
Holding optimal regularization and subsampling fixed, testing if extending boosting to 320 trees at lr=0.025 captures further signal without overfitting.
Since 320 trees showed mild over-boosting compared to 280 (trial 16, 0.5721), testing if an earlier stopping point at 240 trees yields better test performance.
Scaling down learning rate to 0.020 with proportionally more trees (350) around the best regularization parameters to test if finer step sizes yield higher PR-AUC.
Testing a slightly higher learning rate (0.03) with 230 trees since lr=0.02 underperformed, to test if lr=0.025 was near the lower bound.
Testing min_child_weight=8 directly on the current best configuration (trial 16, 0.5721) to check if slightly tighter leaf constraints improve upon min_child_weight=7.
Testing min_child_weight=6 to complete the sensitivity check between 6, 7 (best: 0.5721), and 8 (0.5712).
Testing reg_alpha=0.28 between the 0.20 peak (0.5721) and 0.40 (0.5712) to see if a slightly stronger sparsity constraint improves performance.
Testing n_estimators=265 between 240 (0.5714) and 280 (0.5721) to check if the boosting sequence peaks slightly earlier than 280.
Testing reg_lambda=5.8 near the peak at 6.0 (0.5721) and above 5.0 (0.5716) with all other optimal parameters to see if slight reduction in L2 penalty is optimal.

history.rationale: Initial baseline configuration using moderate depth, learning rate, and regularisation to establish a performance benchmark.
Trial 1 scored 0.5534; testing a shallower tree with higher min_child_weight to reduce potential overfitting on rare positive classes.
Trials 1-2 tested shallow-to-medium trees around ~0.553; testing deeper interactions with max_depth=6 and lower learning rate to capture complex feature relationships.
Trial 3 improved to 0.5559 with deeper trees and lower learning rate; testing max_depth=7 and slightly more trees to see if deeper splits yield further gains.
Trial 3 (depth 6) beat depth 7 (Trial 4) and depth 4 (Trial 1); evaluating depth 5 to pinpoint the sweet spot between depth 4 and 6.
Trial 3 is best at 0.5559 with depth 6; exploring a lower learning rate of 0.02 with more estimators (450) to see if more gradual gradient steps improve precision.
Trial 3 leads with 0.5559; increasing min_child_weight from 2 to 4 to prevent fitting rare spurious positive patterns in depth-6 leaves.
Trial 7 achieved our new best of 0.5575 by increasing min_child_weight to 4; testing min_child_weight=6 to see if stronger minimum leaf support continues to help.
Increasing min_child_weight from 2 (0.5559) to 4 (0.5575) and 6 (0.5629) produced huge gains; testing min_child_weight=8 to probe further along this strong gradient.
Trial 8 with min_child_weight=6 achieved 0.5629 while weight=8 dropped to 0.5585; testing min_child_weight=5 to locate the exact optimum between 4 and 6.
Min_child_weight=6 (0.5629) outperformed 5 (0.5567) and 8 (0.5585); testing min_child_weight=7 to see if the peak lies between 6 and 8.
Trial 11 peaked at 0.5634 with min_child_weight=7 at depth 6; testing depth 7 with this stronger leaf constraint to see if deeper branches now generalize well.
Depth 7 dropped to 0.5577 compared to depth 6 (0.5634); testing depth 5 with min_child_weight=7 to verify depth 6 is indeed the global depth optimum.
Holding the best configuration (depth 6, min_child_weight 7) fixed, testing lower feature subsampling (0.60) to decorrelate individual trees.
Colsample 0.60 gave 0.5632 and 0.75 gave 0.5634; testing colsample_bytree=0.85 to see if higher feature coverage per split helps.
Colsample 0.85 deteriorated sharply (0.5541) while 0.60 and 0.75 were both ~0.563; testing colsample_bytree=0.70 to check intermediate optimal point.
With colsample=0.75 established as best (0.5634), testing higher subsample=0.90 to provide more training data per tree.
Subsample=0.90 degraded performance to 0.5572; testing lower subsample=0.70 to check if stronger row subsampling improves validation PR-AUC.
With subsample=0.80 and colsample=0.75 locked in, testing a lower learning rate 0.02 with 450 trees under min_child_weight=7.
lr=0.02 with 450 trees underperformed; testing slightly fewer trees (250) at lr=0.03 to see if 300 was slightly overfit.
Reducing n_estimators from 300 (0.5634) to 250 increased score to 0.5659; probing n_estimators=200 to test if earlier stopping improves PR-AUC further.
Decreasing trees from 250 (0.5659) to 200 (0.5673) yielded steady improvement; testing n_estimators=160 to find where underfitting begins.
Trial 21 (200 trees: 0.5673) beat 160 (0.5643) and 250 (0.5659); testing n_estimators=210 to bracket the exact peak.
200 trees (0.5673) beat 210 (0.5669); testing n_estimators=190 to check if the optimum is slightly below 200.
With trees tuned to 200 (0.5673), testing higher L2 regularization (reg_lambda=3.0 vs 1.5) to curb leaf weight magnitudes.
reg_lambda=3.0 hurt performance (0.5634 vs 0.5673); testing lower L2 regularization (reg_lambda=0.5) to allow more expressive leaf weights.
reg_lambda=1.5 (0.5673) clearly beat 0.5 (0.5586) and 3.0 (0.5634); testing reg_lambda=1.0 to fine-tune L2 regularization.
reg_lambda=1.5 is confirmed optimal; now testing a lower L1 penalty (reg_alpha=0.01 vs 0.05) to see if less feature sparsity improves score.
reg_alpha=0.01 decreased performance (0.5631); testing slightly stronger L1 regularization (reg_alpha=0.10) to see if pruning weak feature weights improves generalization.
Final trial fine-tuning effective step size: testing learning_rate=0.032 and 195 trees around the best configuration of Trial 21.
